notes.definition: A giant covalent structure is a huge network of atoms in which every atom is joined to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. Substances with giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting and boiling points.
explanation: In a giant covalent structure (sometimes called a macromolecule or giant molecular lattice), there are no separate small molecules. Instead, a very large number of atoms are all linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds, forming a continuous network that extends in all directions. The structure has no fixed size: a bigger crystal simply contains more atoms joined in the same pattern.

Because all the atoms are held by strong covalent bonds, substances with giant covalent structures are solids at room temperature and have very high melting and boiling points. To melt or boil them, many strong covalent bonds must be broken (overcome), and this needs a very large amount of energy. This is different from simple molecular substances, where melting and boiling only overcome the weak intermolecular forces between molecules and no covalent bonds are broken.

You need to know three examples. Diamond and graphite are both forms of carbon. In diamond each carbon atom is bonded to four others, and in graphite each carbon atom is bonded to three others in layers. Silicon dioxide (silica, SiO₂), the main compound in sand, is the third example. In silicon dioxide each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms, which gives the ratio of one silicon to two oxygen in the formula SiO₂.

Carbon dioxide (CO₂) and silicon dioxide (SiO₂) have similar formulae, but very different structures. Carbon dioxide is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them, so it is a gas at room temperature. Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure, so it is a hard solid that melts at about 1700 °C. This shows that you cannot predict the properties of a substance from its formula alone: you need to know its structure.

You should be able to recognise a giant covalent structure from a diagram. Look for atoms that are all connected to each other by covalent bonds (drawn as lines) with no breaks between separate molecules, and bonds that continue off the edges of the diagram to show the structure carries on. There are no ions (no charges), and no separate molecules. Most giant covalent substances, such as diamond and silicon dioxide, do not conduct electricity because they have no free charged particles; graphite is the exception because it has delocalised electrons.
keyFacts: In a giant covalent structure, all atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds.
Giant covalent substances are solids with very high melting and boiling points.
Melting or boiling them requires many strong covalent bonds to be broken, which needs a lot of energy.
Examples: diamond, graphite (both carbon) and silicon dioxide (silica, SiO₂).
In silicon dioxide each Si atom forms 4 covalent bonds to O atoms and each O atom forms 2 bonds to Si atoms.
Giant covalent structures contain no separate molecules and no ions.
Carbon dioxide is a simple molecular gas but silicon dioxide is a giant covalent solid.
Diamond and silicon dioxide do not conduct electricity; graphite does because it has delocalised electrons.

keyTerms.definition: A continuous network of atoms in which every atom is joined to others by strong covalent bonds, with no separate molecules.
A strong bond formed by a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms.
SiO₂, a giant covalent compound found in sand, in which each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid. It is very high for giant covalent substances.
Weak forces between separate molecules. Giant covalent structures do not have separate molecules, so melting them is not about intermolecular forces.

workedExamples.title: Deducing the formula from a structure
workedExamples.question: In a giant covalent structure, each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms. Deduce the formula of the compound.
steps: Each Si atom has 4 Si–O bonds. Each O atom has 2 Si–O bonds.
Every bond joins one Si to one O, so for one Si atom there are 4 bonds, shared out between oxygen atoms that each use 2 of their bonds on silicon.
4 bonds ÷ 2 bonds per oxygen = 2 oxygen atoms per silicon atom.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a very high melting point
workedExamples.question: Silicon dioxide melts at 1710 °C. Explain why its melting point is so high.
steps: Identify the structure: silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure.
Describe the bonding: every atom is joined to other atoms by strong covalent bonds.
Say what happens on melting: many strong covalent bonds must be broken.
Link to energy: this needs a lot of energy, so a very high temperature is needed.
workedExamples.answer: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure; melting it requires breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs a large amount of energy.

diagrams.title: Silicon dioxide: a giant covalent structure
diagrams.caption: A flattened two-dimensional model of silicon dioxide. Each silicon atom is joined to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom to two silicon atoms by strong covalent bonds. Dashed bonds show the network continues in all directions. In the real substance the network is three-dimensional.

diagrams.title: Small molecules compared with a giant covalent structure
diagrams.caption: Left: separate CO₂ molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them. Right: a giant covalent network in which every atom is bonded to its neighbours. Melting the giant structure requires breaking strong covalent bonds.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think giant covalent substances have high melting points because of strong intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.right: In fact giant covalent structures have no separate molecules, so there are no intermolecular forces to overcome. Their high melting points are due to the many strong covalent bonds that must be broken.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that because SiO₂ and CO₂ have similar formulae they have similar properties.
misconceptions.right: In fact CO₂ is a small molecule (a gas at room temperature) and SiO₂ is a giant covalent structure (a solid that melts at about 1700 °C). Structure, not formula, decides the properties.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all covalent substances have low melting points.
misconceptions.right: In fact only simple molecular covalent substances have low melting points. Giant covalent substances have very high melting points.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all giant covalent substances conduct electricity because graphite does.
misconceptions.right: In fact diamond and silicon dioxide do not conduct electricity. Graphite conducts only because it has delocalised electrons.

realWorld: Sand is mostly silicon dioxide; it is melted at very high temperatures to make glass.
Silica bricks and other silica-based materials are used to line furnaces because they withstand very high temperatures.
Diamond is used on the tips of cutting tools and drills because its giant covalent structure makes it extremely hard.
examTips: Use the phrase 'many strong covalent bonds must be broken' and add 'which requires a lot of energy' to gain both marks when explaining a high melting point.
Never mention intermolecular forces when explaining the melting point of a giant covalent substance; examiners treat this as a contradiction.
Learn the three named examples (diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide) so you can identify and name them.
When given a diagram, check whether there are separate molecules (simple molecular), charges (ionic) or a continuous network of bonds (giant covalent).
summary: Giant covalent structures are networks in which all atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds.
They are solids with very high melting and boiling points.
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt or boil them.
Examples are diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide (SiO₂).
They contain no separate molecules, so there are no intermolecular forces to overcome.
Recognise them in diagrams by a continuous network of bonds extending off the edges.

flashcards.front: How many silicon atoms is each oxygen atom bonded to in SiO₂?
Why is CO₂ a gas but SiO₂ a solid?

flashcards.front: Are there intermolecular forces in a giant covalent structure?
flashcards.back: No. There are no separate molecules; all atoms are linked by covalent bonds.
No. It has no free electrons or ions.

flashcards.front: Which giant covalent substance conducts electricity?

questions.question: Which substance has a giant covalent structure?
markScheme: 1 mark: Silicon dioxide
questions.explanation: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure. Carbon dioxide and water are small molecules and sodium chloride is ionic.

questions.question: What type of bonding holds the atoms together in a giant covalent structure?
markScheme: 1 mark: Strong covalent bonds
questions.explanation: All the atoms in a giant covalent structure are linked by strong covalent bonds (shared pairs of electrons).

questions.question: Which property is typical of a substance with a giant covalent structure?
markScheme: 1 mark: Very high melting point
questions.explanation: Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt a giant covalent substance, so its melting point is very high.

questions.question: Which two forms of carbon have giant covalent structures?
markScheme: 1 mark: Diamond and graphite
questions.explanation: Diamond and graphite are both forms of the element carbon with giant covalent structures. Methane, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide are small molecules.

questions.question: What must happen for silicon dioxide to melt?
options: Weak intermolecular forces between SiO₂ molecules are overcome
Ionic bonds between silicon ions and oxide ions are broken
Many strong covalent bonds between atoms are broken
Delocalised electrons are released from the structure
markScheme: 1 mark: Many strong covalent bonds between atoms are broken
questions.explanation: Silicon dioxide has no separate molecules, so there are no intermolecular forces. It is not ionic. Melting requires breaking strong covalent bonds.

questions.question: In silicon dioxide, how many oxygen atoms is each silicon atom covalently bonded to?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Each silicon atom forms four covalent bonds, one to each of four oxygen atoms. Each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms, giving the 1 : 2 ratio in SiO₂.

questions.question: A substance is a hard solid, has a melting point of over 1500 °C and does not conduct electricity when solid or molten. What is its most likely structure?
markScheme: 1 mark: Giant covalent
questions.explanation: A very high melting point rules out simple molecules. Ionic compounds conduct when molten and metals conduct when solid, so the substance is most likely giant covalent.

questions.question: Which description fits a diagram of a giant covalent structure?
options: Positive and negative ions arranged in a regular lattice
Small groups of atoms with gaps between each group
Atoms all joined by covalent bonds in a network that continues off the edges
Positive ions surrounded by a sea of electrons
markScheme: 1 mark: Atoms all joined by covalent bonds in a network that continues off the edges
questions.explanation: A continuous network of covalently bonded atoms is giant covalent. The other options describe ionic, simple molecular and metallic structures.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide sublimes at −78 °C but silicon dioxide melts at 1710 °C. Which is the best explanation?
options: Silicon atoms are heavier than carbon atoms
The covalent bonds in SiO₂ are much stronger than those in CO₂
CO₂ is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, whereas SiO₂ is a giant structure in which strong covalent bonds must be broken
SiO₂ is ionic but CO₂ is covalent
markScheme: 1 mark: CO₂ is made of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces, whereas SiO₂ is a giant structure in which strong covalent bonds must be broken
questions.explanation: The difference is structural. Changing the state of CO₂ only overcomes weak intermolecular forces, but melting SiO₂ breaks strong covalent bonds. Both have strong covalent bonds, and neither is ionic.

questions.question: A student writes: 'Diamond has a high melting point because it has strong intermolecular forces.' Which correction is right?
options: Diamond has weak intermolecular forces, so its melting point is low
Diamond has no intermolecular forces to overcome; melting it requires breaking strong covalent bonds
Diamond has a high melting point because it contains ionic bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: Diamond has no intermolecular forces to overcome; melting it requires breaking strong covalent bonds
questions.explanation: Diamond is a giant covalent structure with no separate molecules. Its high melting point is due to the many strong covalent bonds that must be broken.

questions.question: Give the chemical name of silica.
markScheme: 1 mark: silicon dioxide (SiO₂)
questions.explanation: Silica is the common name for silicon dioxide, the main compound in sand.

questions.question: Describe the bonding in a substance with a giant covalent structure.
markScheme: 1 mark: all (very many) atoms are linked to other atoms
1 mark: by strong covalent bonds (in a continuous network)
questions.explanation: The key words are 'all atoms', 'strong covalent bonds' and 'network'.

questions.question: State why substances with giant covalent structures are solids at room temperature.
acceptedAnswers: lot of energy needed to break bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: all atoms are held by strong covalent bonds that need a lot of energy to break (so the melting point is very high)
questions.explanation: Room temperature is far below the melting points of giant covalent substances because their covalent bonds need a lot of energy to break.

questions.question: Explain why silicon dioxide has a very high melting point.
markScheme: 1 mark: giant covalent structure / many strong covalent bonds
1 mark: (which must be broken and) need a lot of energy to break
questions.explanation: Two marking points: identify the strong covalent bonds and say that a lot of energy is needed to break them.

questions.question: Explain why silicon dioxide does not conduct electricity.
acceptedAnswers: no charged particles free to move
markScheme: 1 mark: all outer electrons are used in covalent bonds
1 mark: so there are no free (delocalised) electrons or ions to carry charge
questions.explanation: To conduct, a substance needs charged particles that can move. Silicon dioxide has neither delocalised electrons nor ions.

questions.question: A diagram shows a substance with atoms joined by covalent bonds in a regular pattern, with bonds continuing off every edge and no charges shown. Identify the type of structure and give one reason from the diagram.
markScheme: 1 mark: giant covalent structure
1 mark: any one: bonds continue off the edges (very large network); no separate molecules; no charges (not ionic)
questions.explanation: A continuous network extending in all directions shows a giant structure; covalent bonds and no charges show it is covalent rather than ionic.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a gas at room temperature but silicon dioxide (SiO₂) is a solid with a very high melting point. Explain this difference in terms of structure and bonding.
markScheme: 1 mark: CO₂ consists of small molecules with weak intermolecular forces between them (little energy to overcome)
1 mark: SiO₂ has a giant covalent structure
1 mark: so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, needing a lot of energy
questions.explanation: Both compounds contain covalent bonds, but only in SiO₂ must covalent bonds be broken to change state. In CO₂ only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.question: Explain why it is incorrect to describe silicon dioxide as being made of SiO₂ molecules.
markScheme: 1 mark: silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure / network with no separate molecules
1 mark: the formula SiO₂ only shows the ratio of Si to O atoms (1 : 2)
questions.explanation: In a giant structure the formula is a ratio, not the composition of a molecule, because the network extends in all directions.

questions.question: Silicon dioxide melts at 1710 °C. Carbon dioxide changes from solid to gas at −78 °C. Calculate the difference between these two temperatures.
questions.explanation: Subtracting a negative number adds it: 1710 + 78 = 1788 °C. A common error is 1710 − 78 = 1632.

questions.question: How many covalent bonds does each silicon atom form in silicon dioxide?
markScheme: 1 mark: 4
questions.explanation: Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms.

questions.question: A small crystal of silicon dioxide contains 3000 silicon atoms. Using the formula SiO₂, how many oxygen atoms does it contain?
questions.explanation: The formula shows two oxygen atoms for every silicon atom, so 3000 × 2 = 6000.

questions.question:
In silicon dioxide, each silicon atom forms four covalent bonds to oxygen atoms. Each Si–O bond joins exactly one silicon atom to one oxygen atom.
Calculate the number of Si–O bonds in a sample containing 500 silicon atoms (ignore atoms at the surface).
markScheme: 1 mark: each Si forms 4 bonds and each bond contains one Si atom
questions.explanation: Every Si–O bond contains exactly one silicon atom, so counting bonds from the silicon side counts each bond once: 500 × 4 = 2000. Multiplying by 4 and by 2 would double count.

questions.question: Silicon dioxide is used to line furnaces that operate at very high temperatures. Describe the structure and bonding in silicon dioxide and explain why it is suitable for this use.
markScheme: Indicative content: giant covalent structure; each silicon atom covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms; each oxygen bonded to two silicon atoms; strong covalent bonds; continuous network in three dimensions; no separate molecules; to melt it many strong covalent bonds must be broken; needs a lot of energy; so very high melting point; so it stays solid at furnace temperatures.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of giant covalent structure and strong covalent bonds, linked logically to a very high melting point and suitability for the furnace.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'it has strong bonds' or 'high melting point' with limited explanation.
questions.explanation: Good answers describe the network of strong covalent bonds and explain that breaking many of them needs a lot of energy, so the lining does not melt.

questions.question:
Compare the structure, bonding and properties of carbon dioxide and silicon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide: gas at room temperature, sublimes at −78 °C, does not conduct electricity.
Silicon dioxide: hard solid, melts at 1710 °C, does not conduct electricity.
markScheme: Indicative content: both are compounds of a group 4 element with oxygen; both contain strong covalent bonds (shared pairs of electrons). Carbon dioxide: small molecules; each molecule CO₂; weak intermolecular forces between molecules; little energy needed to overcome them; so low sublimation point and gas at room temperature; covalent bonds not broken when it changes state. Silicon dioxide: giant covalent structure; each Si bonded to 4 O, each O to 2 Si; no separate molecules; many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt; lots of energy; very high melting point; hard. Both do not conduct electricity because there are no free electrons or ions; all outer electrons used in bonding.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed comparison of both substances covering structure, bonding and at least two properties, with clear reasoning about what is overcome on changing state, and similarities as well as differences.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes the structures of both with some explanation of the difference in melting point, but limited comparison or one property not explained.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both substances, with little reasoning.
questions.explanation: A strong answer is comparative, explaining that state changes in CO₂ overcome weak intermolecular forces while melting SiO₂ breaks strong covalent bonds, and that neither conducts because there are no free charged particles.

questions.question: Name the type of structure in which every atom is joined to other atoms by covalent bonds in a continuous network.
markScheme: 1 mark: giant covalent (structure)
questions.explanation: This is the definition of a giant covalent structure, sometimes called a macromolecular structure.

questions.question: Silicon dioxide is the main compound in which everyday material?
markScheme: 1 mark: Sand
questions.explanation: Sand is mainly silicon dioxide (silica). Salt is sodium chloride, chalk is calcium carbonate and plastics are polymers.

questions.question: Suggest why diamond and silicon dioxide are both very hard.
markScheme: 1 mark: both are giant covalent structures
1 mark: every atom is held in place by strong covalent bonds which are difficult to break
questions.explanation: To scratch or break these materials, many strong covalent bonds would have to be broken, so they are very hard.
